title: The deathbed test
hookLine: Ignatius suggests weighing your choice from your deathbed

cards: There's a decision on the table. A job, a move, a yes or a no to someone. The list of pros and cons has been written twice, and it comes out even.
Nothing inside is pulling hard either way. Ignatius has a tool for exactly this moment. Stop looking at the choice from where you're standing now, he says.
Look at it from the very end of your life, from the bed you'll die in. It sounds grim. Some people find it oddly calming.

teach.b: The deathbed test sits in the part of the Exercises about making a choice, which Ignatius calls an election. He describes three times when a person might choose.
Sometimes God moves the will so clearly there's no doubting it. Sometimes the choice becomes clear through yesterday's movements, consolation and desolation.
And sometimes it's a calm time, nothing stirring, and a person has to use their reason. For that calm time he offers a few tests.
First, think of someone you've never met, whom you wish every good, and ask what you'd advise them. Then follow your own advice.

teach.h: WHAT WOULD I WISH, AT THE END?
teach.b: Second, today's test: consider, as if at the point of death, what you would then wish you had decided, and decide that way now. Third, picture yourself before God at the judgment and ask the same question.
The hope is that much of what pulls at a decision, what people will think, what's comfortable this year, goes quiet at the end, and what's left is simple. Did I love? Did I serve?
Ecclesiasticus, in the Douay-Rheims, puts it plainly: "In all thy works remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin." This isn't meant to be morbid.
Ignatius sets it right beside the stranger test, which is gentle and practical, and both lift you out of the middle of the moment.
If thinking about the end ever stirs thoughts of wanting to die, set this test aside and reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or local emergency help.

how: In Ignatian retreats and in spiritual direction, people facing a major decision in a calm time are invited to use Ignatius's tests, including advising a stranger and considering the choice as if at the point of death.

games.why: for a calm time, he offers tests like this one: look from the end, and decide now as you'd wish you had then.

practice: Bring to mind one choice in front of you, big or small, and let the two options sit side by side. Let time run forward, gently, to the end of a long life, and look back at this choice from there: which way do you wish you had gone?
Then come back to today, to the chair you're sitting in; if you pray, ask for the courage to choose from there.

wordCard.voice: The deathbed test. Weighing a choice from the end of life, and deciding now the way you would wish you had then. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish: election, a choice. Ignatius's word for a decision made before God.

carryVoice: Your line: from the end. The end of a long life is a steadier place to stand. See you tomorrow.
